advanced-industries.overview: Advanced industries covers engineering-heavy manufacturers: carmakers and their suppliers, aircraft and defense companies, and makers of industrial machinery and equipment. Products take years to design and depend on long, global supply chains, so these companies are shaped by how full their factories are, trade policy and the cost of materials like steel. A large share of their profit often comes from servicing and spare parts after the original sale.
advanced-industries.recap: Deals reshaped the sector. Tata Motors took about 89% of Iveco in a deal worth roughly EUR 3.9 billion, Axon invested $1.2 billion more in Skydio and cut its growth outlook, and LS Power proposed buying out EVgo shareholders at $2.00 a share. Ferrari raised its 2026 revenue outlook to EUR 7.65 billion. Over the weekend, China blocked SoftBank's $5.4 billion purchase of ABB's robotics business in China, and Tesla said it will end Cybertruck production in Texas around mid-2027.

consumer-retail.overview: Consumer and retail covers the companies that make and sell what people buy day to day. That includes stores and online retailers, makers of food, drinks and household products, farm and food businesses, and travel and hospitality companies like airlines and hotels. Consumer spending is about two-thirds of the US economy, so these businesses rise and fall with how confident people feel and how much money they have left after essentials.
consumer-retail.recap: Deals and distress stood out. Organigram agreed to buy Aurora Cannabis for about C$561 million, Spain's Dcoop and Acesur took over olive oil maker Deoleo, and Poundland filed to appoint administrators, putting about 12,000 jobs at risk. Airbnb's revenue rose 19% and it authorized $12 billion more in buybacks, Shopify's revenue rose 32%, and DraftKings fell 22% as its loss widened to $469 million. US airline shares jumped about 4% when crude fell sharply on Monday.

energy-materials.overview: Energy and materials covers the companies that pull resources out of the ground and turn them into fuel, power and raw materials. That includes oil and gas producers, the pipelines, ships and terminals that move their output, refineries and chemical plants, electric utilities and renewable developers, and miners and steelmakers. These are capital-heavy businesses that live with commodity prices they don't control, so returns depend on keeping costs low and investing at the right point in the cycle.
energy-materials.recap: Oil swung on diplomacy. Brent hit about $103.60 on Tuesday, fell on reports Iran had cleared the way for talks, and ended Friday near $98, down more than 16% on the week, while energy shares fell 12%. UK gas averaged 216 pence a therm, 81% above July. BP earned $8.5 billion and Marathon Petroleum $7.4 billion on strong refining margins, QatarEnergy signed a 20-year deal for up to 3 million tonnes a year of Woodside's Louisiana LNG, and Freeport approved a $4.5 billion Arizona copper expansion. On Sunday, debris damaged Aramco's Riyadh tower, and IEA data put 2026 global energy investment near $3.4 trillion.

financial-services.overview: Financial services is the business of managing, lending, investing and moving money. Banks take deposits and make loans, insurers collect premiums to cover risks, asset managers invest on behalf of savers and pension funds, and payments companies handle the flow of money between people and businesses. It is one of the most heavily regulated industries, so how much capital firms must hold and how well they control risk shapes how profitable they can be.
financial-services.recap: Crypto and payments dominated. A $6.3 billion theft from Binance, linked by analysts to North Korean hackers, was called the largest crypto heist on record, and on Friday the US Treasury moved to cut MEXC off from American institutions over alleged illicit flows of at least $16 billion. Fiserv took a $6.45 billion goodwill write-down but doubled its cost-savings target to $1 billion. On Saturday, Berkshire Hathaway reported lower operating profit as insurance underwriting fell 43%, while it bought back $9.6 billion of stock.

healthcare.overview: Healthcare covers the companies that discover, make, pay for and deliver medical care. Drugmakers and biotech firms develop medicines, device makers build everything from surgical tools to heart implants, insurers pay for care, and hospitals and doctors provide it. In the US the system is large and complex, and prices are set through negotiation between manufacturers, insurers and the middlemen between them, so policy and regulation matter as much as science.
healthcare.recap: Drugmakers raised outlooks. Pfizer lifted its 2026 revenue range to $62 billion to $64 billion, Novo Nordisk raised its guidance for the third time as the Wegovy pill reached DKK 5.4 billion, and Moderna returned to profit and lifted its growth outlook to 15% to 25%. Neurocrine's revenue rose 41% and Guardant's 36%. CVS Health plans to split into two public companies by the first half of 2028, and Stevanato warned that lower GLP-1 volumes will slow its 2027 growth.

infrastructure-logistics.overview: Infrastructure and logistics covers the physical networks the rest of the economy runs on. That includes the trucking, rail, shipping and air freight companies that move goods, the developers and builders behind homes, offices and data centers, and the public sector that funds and regulates much of it. These businesses are sensitive to fuel costs and interest rates, because moving goods burns diesel and most buildings are paid for with borrowed money.
infrastructure-logistics.recap: Few stories were filed this week. Uber reported gross bookings up 20% to $59.8 billion, with Freight growing fastest. Only one infrastructure and logistics story was filed this week.

macro.overview: The macro picture covers the forces that move every industry at once: how fast economies are growing, how quickly prices are rising, where central banks set interest rates, and how goods and money flow between countries. When energy costs climb or borrowing gets more expensive, the effects show up in nearly every company's results, so this is the backdrop for reading the rest of the news.
macro.recap: The week ended with stress in markets. The S&P 500 fell 2.7% and the Nasdaq 3.4% after Thursday's 4.4% drop, and the 10-year yield closed the week at 4.86%. October payrolls rose 165,000 against a forecast of about 59,000, while the Bank of England raised its rate to 4% and traders priced about a 68% chance of a December Fed hike. A Democratic sweep in the midterms put tariffs and tech export controls back in play, though changes are unlikely before January. October inflation data is due Tuesday.

tmt.overview: Tech, media and telecom covers the companies behind computing and communication: chipmakers, software and cloud providers, internet platforms like search and social media, entertainment and streaming companies, and the telecom networks that connect everything. Many of these businesses become more profitable as they grow, because serving one more customer costs very little, which is why a handful of very large companies dominate. Much of the sector's investment today is going into the data centers and chips that power AI.
tmt.recap: AI spending worries drove tech. Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum for $115 billion in stock, AMD posted record revenue of $13.4 billion, and Apple, Palantir and AppLovin posted strong growth. But the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell about 12% on Thursday, and Asian chip stocks fell as much as 10% on Friday before US chips rebounded 4.2%. Democratic governors-elect threatened slower data center permitting, and software earnings split, with Cloudflare surging while Atlassian fell more than 15%.

software-cloud.overview: Software and cloud covers the companies that rent computing power over the internet and sell business software as subscriptions. Three giants, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, hold about two thirds of cloud infrastructure spending, and software vendors such as Salesforce, ServiceNow and Fortinet sell on top of them. Demand for AI is lifting growth sharply, but the capital spending needed has turned the largest providers' free cash flow negative.

telecom.overview: Telecom companies build and run the networks that carry voice, data and video: mobile, fixed broadband and the fiber and towers behind them. The industry is moving to 5G and fiber while looking for new revenue from enterprise and AI-driven data demand.

transport-logistics.operatingModel: Asset-heavy carriers earn revenue per mile or per container and live on utilization. Contract rates are set annually while spot rates swing daily; fuel surcharges pass part of fuel cost to shippers with a lag. Brokers are asset-light and earn the spread between shipper and carrier rates.
transport-logistics.overview: Transport and logistics moves goods and people through trucks, trains, ships, planes, warehouses and the brokers that arrange them. It is built from asset-heavy carriers that own vehicles and asset-light intermediaries that sell capacity they do not own. Money is made by keeping assets full and by charging for reliability, with fuel, freight cycles and chokepoints driving the swings. The industry is currently shaped by shipping detours, high fuel costs and large container-ship orderbooks.

travel-hospitality.overview: Travel and hospitality covers the airlines, hotels, cruise lines, booking sites and restaurants that move, host and feed people on trips. Airlines earn thin margins while hotel and restaurant brands earn steadier fees by franchising to owners. Fuel prices, conflict and consumer confidence are the main forces now changing results.
